strengths: Novel problem formulation (token sample complexity) timely for extended-context LLMs with clear measure-theoretic framework
Rigorous theoretical analysis with sophisticated application of empirical process theory (Dudley's entropy integral, symmetrization) handling autocorrelation in self-attention
Refined sub-Gaussian framework capturing token distribution anisotropy through interpretable coupling coefficients (attention horizon H and attention-token coupling Ψ)
Comprehensive multi-level analysis: pointwise convergence, uniform convergence on balls, and moment convergence with explicit dependence on attention geometry and data properties
Novel hardmax asymptotics (Proposition 5.5) revealing symmetry-driven cancellation with exact rates σ/√ln n for Gaussian case

Convincing experimental validation on synthetic Gaussian data showing tight agreement with theory; real data experiments (BigBird on Wikipedia) demonstrating sub-parametric convergence rates β < 1/2 in practice across multiple languages
Reproducible research with open-sourced code and well-documented experimental protocols
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.2 requires exponential n ≥ 4e^{2R²||Σ^{1/2}A||_2²}(1/δ-1) in R and spectral norm; bounds acknowledged as non-sharp with looseness unquantified
Limited scope to single attention layer with fixed parameters; no analysis of deep stacking, residual connections, or layer-wise error propagation despite practical relevance
Theorem 5.3 depends on unknown parameters (Ψ, H); fitted post-hoc in experiments rather than predicted a priori, limiting practical predictive value
Hardmax analysis (Proposition 5.5) restricted to 1D Gaussian case; claimed extensions to non-Gaussian real embeddings justified by intuition ('skewness, kurtosis') rather than rigorous analysis

Limited experimental scope: only BigBird-RoBERTa-base tested (small model); no modern LLMs; measures only mean/covariance convergence, not downstream task performance or actual utility of extended context
Assumes i.i.d. tokens despite acknowledgment that natural text violates this; robustness not rigorously established
Dense presentation with implicit dependencies and complex notation (multiple β parameters) making accessibility and interpretability challenging
Missing practical guidance: convergence rates do not translate to concrete recommendations for context window selection, sparse attention design, or downstream performance guarantees

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Token sample complexity as n increases at fixed parameters is timely and well-motivated given long-context LLM trends
Rigorous mathematical framework: Proper use of measure theory, empirical processes, and extreme value theory with careful handling of technical challenges (non-Lipschitz softmax, dependent Q/K/V)
Attention horizon as unifying concept: Identification of H = ||Σ^(1/2)AΣ^(1/2)||₂ governing convergence, with clear geometric interpretation
Multiple analytical perspectives: Pointwise convergence (Theorem 4.2), moment convergence (Theorem 5.3), and hardmax limit provide complementary insights
Strong experimental validation: Theory-practice agreement on Gaussian data, systematic evaluation across BigBird/BERT layers/languages, convincing downstream task experiments
Practical insights: Demonstration that 25% of keys recover most accuracy; downstream slowdown matches theoretical predictions
Comprehensive treatment: Full proofs in appendix, multiple extensions (covariance, deep composition, compactly supported), honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Theorem 4.2 exponential dependence: e^(8R²||Σ^(1/2)A||²₂) bound is uninformative for realistic radii R; acknowledged issue but not resolved in main result
Sub-parametric rates arbitrarily slow: Exponent β = 1/(2(1+32H²)) approaches 0 for large H; practical convergence becomes impractical in high-horizon regimes
Theory-practice gap: Analysis assumes fixed parameters, but practical transformers train end-to-end; relationship between training-time and inference-time token behavior unexplored
i.i.d. assumption restrictive: Real token sequences have dependencies; theoretical guarantees only for i.i.d. sampling despite empirical evidence for window-based sampling
Hardmax analysis limited: Proposition 5.5 restricted to 1D Gaussian; cancellation phenomenon is Gaussian-specific; condition ||Aσ||₂ ≫ 1 may not hold in practice
Complicated constants limit applicability: Polynomial P in Theorem 5.3, constant q in Theorem 4.2 lack explicit forms; practitioners cannot easily apply bounds
Limited practical guidance: Paper does not explain how to use convergence rates to improve models or allocate computational resources
Incomplete sparse attention analysis: Limited comparison to existing methods (Linformer, Performer); window-based sampling only briefly explored
